questions.question: Which waveform contains only the fundamental frequency with no harmonics?
questions.explanation: A sine wave is the purest waveform — it contains only the fundamental frequency and no harmonic content. All other common waveforms (sawtooth, square, triangle) are combinations of multiple sine waves at different harmonics.

questions.question: A sawtooth wave contains which harmonics?
questions.explanation: A sawtooth wave is harmonically the richest common waveform — it contains all harmonics (both odd and even) at decreasing amplitudes. This gives it a bright, buzzy character ideal as a starting point for subtractive synthesis.

questions.question: What is the correct signal flow in a standard subtractive synthesiser?
questions.explanation: In subtractive synthesis, the oscillator generates the raw waveform with harmonics, the filter removes unwanted harmonics to shape the timbre, and the amplifier controls the final output level. This VCO → VCF → VCA chain is fundamental to the architecture.

questions.question: In an ADSR envelope applied to a filter, what does the Sustain stage control?
options: The cutoff frequency level held while a note is pressed
The time taken for the filter to open fully
The time taken for the filter to close after the note ends
The speed at which the filter drops from its peak
questions.explanation: Sustain is the only ADSR stage measured as a level (not a time). It sets the filter cutoff frequency maintained for as long as the note is held. Attack, Decay, and Release are all time parameters.

questions.question: What happens to a resonant low-pass filter when self-oscillation is reached?
options: The filter generates its own sine wave tone at the cutoff frequency
The filter stops passing all frequencies
The filter begins to pass high frequencies instead
The filter cutoff shifts one octave lower
questions.explanation: When resonance is increased to the point of self-oscillation, the filter feedback becomes so strong that it generates its own pitched tone — a sine wave at the cutoff frequency — even without any input signal.

questions.question: An LFO running at 5Hz applied to oscillator pitch would produce which effect?
questions.explanation: An LFO (Low Frequency Oscillator) below 20Hz modulates a parameter cyclically. At 5Hz applied to pitch, it creates vibrato — a periodic wobble in pitch. Applied to amplitude it would create tremolo instead.

questions.question: A square wave contains only odd harmonics. If the fundamental is the 1st harmonic, how many harmonics are present in the first five odd harmonics?
questions.explanation: The odd harmonics are the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th, and 9th. Counting these gives 5 harmonics. Square and triangle waves share this odd-only harmonic series, which is why they sound more hollow than a sawtooth.

questions.question: How many stages does a standard ADSR envelope have?
questions.explanation: ADSR stands for Attack, Decay, Sustain, Release — four discrete stages. Each stage has a distinct role: Attack (time to peak), Decay (time to sustain level), Sustain (held level), Release (time to silence after note off).

questions.question: A 4-pole low-pass filter (24dB/octave) is set to a cutoff of 1kHz. A signal at 4kHz is how many octaves above the cutoff?
questions.explanation: Each doubling of frequency represents one octave. 1kHz → 2kHz = 1 octave. 2kHz → 4kHz = 2 octaves. At 24dB/octave, the signal at 4kHz would be attenuated by 48dB (2 × 24).

questions.question: Explain the difference between additive and subtractive synthesis.
questions.sampleAnswer: Additive synthesis builds a sound by adding together individual sine waves (harmonics) to create a complex tone. Subtractive synthesis starts with a harmonically rich waveform and removes unwanted harmonics using a filter to shape the timbre.
questions.explanation: Additive synthesis works bottom-up — construct complexity from simple parts. Subtractive synthesis works top-down — start with complexity (sawtooth, square) and carve it down with filters. Subtractive is far more common in hardware and virtual synths because it is computationally cheaper and more intuitive to sculpt.

questions.question: Describe the role of each ADSR envelope stage in shaping the sound of a synthesised string patch.
questions.sampleAnswer: Attack: slow attack time means the sound fades in gradually, mimicking a bow drawing across strings. Decay: short decay as the note settles. Sustain: high sustain level keeps the string tone present while held. Release: moderate release lets the tone fade naturally after the key is lifted.
questions.explanation: A string patch relies heavily on envelope shaping. A fast attack would make it sound like a plucked instrument rather than bowed. Long release prevents an abrupt cut-off. The ADSR envelope can be applied to both the amplifier (volume shape) and the filter (timbral brightness over time).

questions.question: What is resonance on a filter, and how does it affect the sound?
questions.sampleAnswer: Resonance boosts the frequencies around the filter's cutoff point, creating a peak in the frequency response. As resonance increases, this peak becomes more pronounced, giving the sound a ringing, nasal quality. At extreme settings, the filter can self-oscillate.
questions.explanation: Resonance (also called Q or emphasis) feeds some of the filter's output back into its input, amplifying the frequencies near the cutoff. This creates the characteristic 'wah' sweep sound when the cutoff is automated. At maximum resonance, the feedback sustains indefinitely — self-oscillation — generating a pure sine tone.

questions.question: Pulse width modulation (PWM) on a pulse/square wave oscillator changes:
options: The ratio of the high portion to the low portion of the waveform cycle
The number of harmonics from odd-only to all harmonics
questions.explanation: Pulse width (or duty cycle) is the ratio of time the waveform spends in its high state versus its low state. A 50% pulse width is a standard square wave. Narrowing the pulse width changes the harmonic content — introducing even harmonics and creating a thinner, more nasal timbre. Modulating the pulse width over time (PWM) produces the classic animated, chorus-like movement heard in many analogue synthesiser pads.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the unison/detune feature on a synthesiser?
options: To stack multiple slightly detuned copies of the oscillator for a thicker, wider sound
To lock two oscillators to exactly the same frequency
To automatically tune the oscillator to the nearest semitone
To apply vibrato from an internal LFO
questions.explanation: Unison mode duplicates the oscillator voice multiple times and detunes each copy by a small amount (typically measured in cents). The slight pitch differences create phasing and beating between the copies, resulting in a thicker, fatter, wider sound. The more voices and greater detune amount, the bigger the effect — though at the cost of increased CPU usage and potential tuning vagueness.

questions.question: Oscillator sync forces one oscillator (the slave) to:
options: Play at half the frequency of the master oscillator
Use the same waveform shape as the master oscillator
Restart its waveform cycle every time the master oscillator completes a cycle
Match the amplitude envelope of the master oscillator
questions.explanation: In hard oscillator sync, the slave oscillator is forced to reset its waveform to the beginning each time the master completes one full cycle. If the slave is set to a different pitch, its waveform is repeatedly truncated, producing a distinctive harmonically rich, aggressive timbre. Sweeping the slave pitch while synced creates the classic 'sync sweep' lead sound.

questions.question: Ring modulation multiplies two signals together. If oscillator A is at 400 Hz and oscillator B is at 500 Hz, which frequencies appear in the output?
questions.explanation: Ring modulation produces sum and difference frequencies of the two inputs. The sum is 400 + 500 = 900 Hz and the difference is 500 − 400 = 100 Hz. The original input frequencies are removed. When the two inputs are not harmonically related, ring modulation produces metallic, bell-like, or dissonant inharmonic tones.

questions.question: A synthesiser plays a note at 440 Hz. Portamento (glide) is enabled and the next note played is one octave higher. What is the target frequency in Hz?
questions.explanation: One octave higher means doubling the frequency. 440 × 2 = 880 Hz. Portamento causes the pitch to slide smoothly from 440 Hz to 880 Hz over a set glide time rather than jumping instantly. This creates a characteristic sliding effect used in many lead synth patches.

questions.question: A pulse wave oscillator has a pulse width of 25%. What percentage of each cycle does the waveform spend in its low state?
questions.explanation: Pulse width defines the proportion of the cycle spent in the high state. If the pulse width is 25%, the remaining 100% − 25% = 75% is spent in the low state. A 25% pulse width produces a thinner, more nasal tone than a 50% square wave because the asymmetric duty cycle introduces even harmonics.

questions.question: Explain the difference between wavetable synthesis and subtractive synthesis. Why might a sound designer choose wavetable synthesis over subtractive for a particular patch?
questions.sampleAnswer: Subtractive synthesis starts with a fixed waveform (e.g. sawtooth or square) and uses a filter to remove harmonics. Wavetable synthesis stores a table of many different single-cycle waveforms and allows the oscillator to scan through them over time, creating evolving timbral changes that would be impossible with a static oscillator waveform. A sound designer might choose wavetable synthesis for pads or textures that need continuous tonal evolution without relying solely on filter movement.
keyPoints: subtractive uses fixed waveforms plus filter
timbral changes beyond what filtering alone achieves
questions.explanation: Wavetable synthesis dramatically expands the timbral palette available at the oscillator stage. Instead of being limited to sawtooth, square, triangle, and sine, the oscillator can morph through hundreds of different waveshapes. This makes it particularly suited to modern electronic music sound design where evolving, complex textures are needed.

questions.question: Describe what envelope retriggering means and explain how it affects a monophonic synthesiser patch when playing legato (overlapping notes).
questions.sampleAnswer: Envelope retriggering determines whether the ADSR envelope restarts from the beginning of the attack stage each time a new note is played. With retriggering enabled, every new note starts a fresh envelope regardless of whether the previous note is still held. With retriggering disabled (legato mode), playing overlapping notes causes the envelope to continue from its current position — only the pitch changes. This produces a smoother, more connected playing style because subsequent notes skip the attack stage and glide into the new pitch.
keyPoints: pitch changes but envelope does not restart
questions.explanation: Retriggering behaviour is critical for expressive monophonic patches. Lead synth sounds often disable retriggering so that fast legato passages sound fluid rather than stuttered. Combined with portamento, this creates the classic sliding monosynth lead heard in many genres.
